import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c
import numpy as np

import funs
from funs import DSText, umap_text

import spacy

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"

```{python}

docs = (
    pl.read_parquet(ub + "data/agnews_pca.parquet")
    .filter(c.index == "test")
    .select(c.id, c.label, c.text)
    .rename({"id": "doc_id"})
    .sort(c.doc_id)

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
```

```{python}
#| tags: [noclear]
anno = DSText.process(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.text), nlp)
```

### Questions

`docs` and `anno` are the same 200 AG News articles from the last notebook,
50 each labeled `"Business"`, `"Sci/Tech"`, `"Sports"`, or `"World"`. The
last notebook counted words within each article; this one turns each article
into a single point and asks how those points relate to one another. Print
results unless a question says otherwise.

1. Compute the TF-IDF table with `DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01,
max_df=1.0)`, the same call from the last notebook. Print its shape and the
number of distinct lemmas it covers.

```{python}
tfidf = DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=1.0)
print(tfidf.shape)
(
    tfidf
    .select(c.lemma.n_unique())
)
```

2. In the first block, pick two lemmas, `"olympic"` and `"profit"`, pivot
their TF-IDF scores into two columns, filling missing combinations with zero,
join `label` on, and plot every document as its `doc_id`, positioned by these
two scores and colored by `label`. In the second block, filter to the
documents with a nonzero score for both terms. How many are there? Compare
this to the book's `poem`/`novel` example, where authors who write in both
forms show up in the upper-right corner of the plot.

```{python}
scatter_df = (
    tfidf
    .filter(c.lemma.is_in(["olympic", "profit"]))
    .pivot(on="lemma", index="doc_id", values="tfidf")
    .fill_null(0)
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on="doc_id")
)

(
    scatter_df
    .ggplot(aes(c.olympic, c.profit))
    .geom_text(aes(label=c.doc_id, color=c.label), size=6)
)
```

```{python}
(
    scatter_df
    .filter((c.olympic > 0) & (c.profit > 0))
)
```

Zero. Eleven documents (all `Sports`) sit along the `olympic` axis with a
`profit` score of exactly 0, and eleven more (all `Business`) sit along the
`profit` axis with an `olympic` score of exactly 0. The other 178 sit at the
origin, using neither word, and the upper-right corner is empty. The book's
authors write poetry and prose in mixed proportions, so some of them land
away from both axes. `olympic` and `profit` belong to two unrelated news
beats, so no article in this corpus has a reason to use both.

3. The TF-IDF matrix from question 1 has a row for every document and a
column for every lemma, but `tfidf` only stores the nonzero entries, one per
row. Use that to compute the size of the full matrix (documents times
lemmas), the percentage of its entries that are exactly zero, and the
average number of nonzero terms per document.

```{python}
(
    tfidf
    .select(
        n_docs = c.doc_id.n_unique(),
        n_lemmas = c.lemma.n_unique(),
        n_nonzero = pl.len()
    )
    .with_columns(
        pct_zero = (100 * (1 - c.n_nonzero / (c.n_docs * c.n_lemmas))).round(1),
        avg_nonzero = (c.n_nonzero / c.n_docs).round(1)
    )
)
```

97.4% of the matrix is zero. On average each of these 200 short wire
articles uses only about 24 of the corpus's 917 lemmas, a concrete number
behind the chapter's description of a TF-IDF matrix as a *sparse
embedding*.

4. Build a 2D UMAP projection of the corpus with `umap_text`, using
`min_df=0.01` and `max_df=0.5` as the chapter does, and plot each document's
`label` at its projected position, colored by `label`. Does the plot show
four clean, separated clusters the way the book's biography pages did?

```{python}
umap_full = (
    anno
    .pipe(
        umap_text,
        doc_id=c.doc_id,
        term_id=c.lemma,
        n_components=2,
        min_df=0.01,
        max_df=0.5,
        random_state=42
    )
    .predict(full=True)
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on="doc_id")
)

(
    umap_full
    .ggplot(aes(c.dr0, c.dr1))
    .geom_text(aes(label=c.label, color=c.label), size=6)
)
```

No. The four labels form loose, overlapping neighborhoods instead of four
separate blobs. A `Sports` patch in the upper left sits right next to a
`World` patch, and `Business` and `Sci/Tech` interleave through the middle of
the plot, far from the clean separation of the chapter's biography pages.
Question 7 measures this directly with the full-dimensional distances.

5. Compute the pairwise angle distance between every pair of documents with
`DSText.compute_distances(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)` and save it as
`text_dist`. Each pair is stored once, in `doc_id < doc_id2` order. Stack the
table with a copy of itself with the two ID columns swapped, so that every
document appears in the `doc_id` column with a row for every other document,
and print the shape of the result.

```{python}
text_dist = DSText.compute_distances(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)

text_dist_both = pl.concat([
    text_dist,
    text_dist.select(doc_id=c.doc_id2, doc_id2=c.doc_id, distance=c.distance)
])
text_dist_both.shape
```

6. The last notebook's `doc120027` was Michael Phelps's "Giddy Phelps
Touches Gold" article. Find its five closest matches in `text_dist_both`.

```{python}
(
    text_dist_both
    .filter(c.doc_id == "doc120027")
    .sort(c.distance)
    .head(5)
)
```

The closest match, `doc120159` at distance 1.04, is titled "Phelps Eyes
Fourth Gold," a second wire article about the same swimmer at the same
Olympics. It sits well ahead of the next four matches (all above 1.30),
which are Olympic articles about other athletes and events.

7. Find the single nearest neighbor of every document at once, and report
what proportion of documents have a nearest neighbor sharing their own
`label`, both overall and broken down by `label`.

```{python}
nn = (
    text_dist_both
    .sort(c.doc_id, c.distance)
    .group_by(c.doc_id, maintain_order=True)
    .head(1)
)

nn_labeled = (
    nn
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .join(
        docs.select(pl.col("doc_id").alias("doc_id2"), pl.col("label").alias("label2")),
        on=c.doc_id2
    )
)

print(
    nn_labeled
    .select((c.label == c.label2).mean())
)

(
    nn_labeled
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(n=pl.len(), n_same=(c.label == c.label2).sum())
)
```

70% of documents (140 of 200) have a same-topic nearest neighbor under the
full-dimensional angle distance, well above the 25% expected from random
guessing among four labels. That is a sharper picture than the loose
neighborhoods of question 4's 2D projection, because collapsing hundreds of
dimensions to two throws away some of the structure that separates the
topics. `Sports` is easiest to match (80%, 40 of 50) and `Sci/Tech` hardest
(56%, 28 of 50).

8. In the first block, find the single closest pair of documents in the
whole corpus under the angle distance. In the second block, print both
articles' full text. What makes them so close?

```{python}
closest_pair = (
    text_dist
    .sort(c.distance)
    .head(1)
)
closest_pair
```

```{python}
print(
    docs
    .filter(c.doc_id == closest_pair.item(0, "doc_id"))
    .item(0, "text")
)
print(
    docs
    .filter(c.doc_id == closest_pair.item(0, "doc_id2"))
    .item(0, "text")
)
```

At a distance of 0.37, by far the smallest in the corpus (the next-closest
pair is at 0.77), `doc120195` and `doc120199` are two Reuters versions of the
same story about Medtronic's quarterly earnings. Apart from the headline,
their texts differ by a single word ("amid" against "on"). The angle
distance has found a near-duplicate, not a coincidence of vocabulary.

9. `text_dist_both` also contains pairs at the maximum possible distance,
$\pi/2$, meaning the two documents share no filtered vocabulary at all. In
the first block, find the document involved in the most such pairs. In the
second block, print that document's text and look at its top TF-IDF terms to
explain why.

```{python}
lonely = (
    text_dist_both
    .filter((c.distance - np.pi / 2).abs() < 1e-9)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(n=pl.len())
    .sort(c.n, descending=True)
)
(
    lonely
    .head(5)
)
```

```{python}
loneliest = (
    lonely
    .item(0, "doc_id")
)
print(
    docs
    .filter(c.doc_id == loneliest)
    .item(0, "text")
)

(
    DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=0.5)
    .filter(c.doc_id == loneliest)
    .sort(c.tfidf, descending=True)
    .head(5)
)
```

`doc120178` shares no filtered vocabulary with 162 of the other 199
documents, over 80% of the corpus. It is not a broken row. It is a short
article (16 surviving terms) about the cyclist Leontien Zijlaard-van
Moorsel, and spaCy's tokenizer splits her name into three tokens
(`Zijlaard`, `van`, `Moorsel`), each of which appears in only one other
document. Those rare tokens get the highest IDF weight the `min_df` filter
allows and dominate the document's normalized direction. Unless another
article mentions this cyclist by name, the angle between the two vectors
lands at the maximum. A short document built around one uncommon proper name
is an outlier almost by construction, so be careful about reading too much
into any single document's distance to the rest of a corpus.
